Houston City Council: local ideal points, 2003–2026

Pooled roll calls · Provisional historical analysis

Published

September 25, 2026

This analysis places 67 Houston officials who cast qualifying council votes between 2003 and 2026 on one pooled voting scale. The tabs follow elected councils, with two-year terms before 2016 and four-year terms thereafter, and show each council on the same estimated axis. The latest council runs from Plummer and Pollard to Flickinger and Huffman. Among members serving in 2021–2026, the pooled ordering closely matches a separate modern-only fit and tracks documented party affiliation and district presidential voting. The cross-era alignment remains provisional, however. The plots present the requested 24-year pooled estimates, not a settled historical ranking. Estimation and that limitation are detailed in the technical appendix; the separate 2021–2025 report remains available.

Dataset and construction

The input is the 2003–2026 candidate ZIP from the shared Drive folder, byte-identical to council-votes/houston/houston_rollcalls_2003_2026.zip at commit 8840cca (SHA-256 89294d18539fdccfeada276cd810f8120e82bf5e6f6b45e0966e1acee92ea0fd). It contains 29,384 actions and 475,292 member rows, dated September 2003 to May 2026. Jacob labels 549 actions as scaling-eligible because at least two members voted each way. Requiring each person to cast at least seven qualifying yea/nay votes leaves all 549 actions, 67 members, and 8,268 observed votes. Seven names fall below the threshold in the source matrix, including two one-vote variants and former mayor Lee P. Brown, who appears on only two qualifying actions.

The mayor votes as part of the council. Today’s 17 voting officials are the mayor, eleven district members, and five at-large members; the earlier council had nine district seats (Houston’s 2003 almanac). A person is missing, not coded nay, when absent, departed, or omitted from an explicit roll call. Only actions with at least two recorded yeas and two recorded nays enter the scale. Most council business is unanimous or close to it, so these actions are a selected subset of policy decisions rather than a summary of everything the council did. The bar chart shows how many qualifying disagreements are observed for each elected council.

The period tabs follow the terms produced by Houston’s regular elections. The city had two-year elected terms through 2014–2015; voters adopted four-year terms effective January 2016 (Houston’s 2003 almanac; 2016 city financial report). Terms begin January 2 (City Council), and the City Secretary’s election record identifies the election years. The first tabbed council was elected in 2001 but appears only in September 2003; the 2023-elected council is observed only through May 2026. A vacancy or special election changes a member within an elected council, not the council’s term boundary.

All five actions we previously verified by hand are present in the new ZIP and are not appended again. Three need analysis-side corrections against our saved page transcriptions: the June 2024 ordinance omits Castex-Tatum’s later return; two late-2025 motions truncate explicit 17-person roll calls after nine names. The corrected cells are listed in Results/Houston-full/verified_overrides.csv; the upstream ZIP is untouched. The separate houston_balance_votes.csv is superseded and is not merged. Yea is 1, nay is 0, and all other responses remain missing.

Results

The council elected in 2023 (2024–2027 term)

An ideal point summarizes voting similarity on contested roll calls: nearby members usually take the same side; distant members more often oppose one another. The pooled fit gives each of the 67 retained officials one position across all the years in which that person appears. The chart shows everyone with a qualifying vote so far in the council elected in 2023; their positions are estimated from the entire 2003–2026 matrix. Amy Peck is displayed on the positive side by convention. The units are specific to this Houston sample and cannot be compared numerically with other cities.

The positive end remains Republican-affiliated; Plummer, Pollard, Jackson, and Thomas are at the negative end. Most positions in the middle overlap. The pooled and separate 2021–2026 fits correlate 0.981 across their 25 shared officials. This is a useful consistency check, not independent evidence: the votes overlap heavily.

Earlier four-year councils

Each tab draws the people who recorded a qualifying vote during that elected council’s term at their pooled position. Members appear in more than one tab if reelected or otherwise continuing; there is no separate re-estimation or rescaling. The mayor is a square. Party colors use evidence assembled for the modern council; older officials without comparable evidence are gray. Conditional intervals omit uncertainty about the alternative cross-era alignment.

The elected councils contribute very different numbers of divided actions: only two from the observed tail of 2002–2003, versus 116 in 2020–2023. The pooled positive extreme among earlier officials is Addie Wiseman (4.04), followed by Helena Brown (3.44); Jolanda “Jo” Jones (-1.04) lies toward the negative end. These are voting positions, not independently researched ideological labels. Even where members serve across elections, the uneven supply of informative votes limits cross-council comparisons.

Individual members and policy controversies

Among recent members, Fred Flickinger (2.36), Greg Travis (1.19), Mike Knox (1.30), and Mary Nan Huffman (1.36) sit at the positive end. Flickinger’s interval is relatively wide because he entered office in 2024. Letitia Plummer (-1.15), Edward Pollard (-0.97), Tarsha Jackson (-0.90), and Tiffany Thomas (-0.73) sit at the negative end. The following examples, retained from the independently checked 2021–2025 analysis, show what some of their opposing votes concerned:

  • Conservation districts (April 2023): rules intended to slow redevelopment and displacement in historically Black and Latino neighborhoods passed 13–4; Peck, Martin, Huffman, and Knox opposed the restrictions on property owners. Houston Chronicle; Houston Public Media
  • Gun buyback funding (August 2022): $539,000 in federal relief money for gift cards passed 12–4 over Peck, Huffman, Knox, and Kubosh, amid disagreement about whether anonymous buybacks reduce gun crime. KPRC
  • Property tax rate (September 2023): council cut the rate slightly, though higher appraisals increased total revenue. Peck, Huffman, Knox, and Kubosh voted no on the 12–4 levy. Houston Chronicle
  • Disaster-recovery housing (August 2025): an amendment moved $50 million of federal storm-recovery funds from power generation to home repair. The amended plan passed 12–3, with Peck, Flickinger, and Huffman opposed. KPRC
  • I-45 right-of-way sale (January 2025): the city sold land by White Oak Bayou to TxDOT for the contested highway project. The recorded 9–7 split placed Plummer, Pollard, Jackson, Thomas, Kamin, Evans-Shabazz, and Castillo in opposition; Peck, Huffman, Flickinger, and Mayor Whitmire supported the sale. ABC13

These cases suggest a spectrum involving fiscal and land-use regulation, spending priorities, and highway development. They illustrate the dimension; they do not establish that every divided vote has the same policy meaning. Tallies above follow the official roll calls; news summaries occasionally differ.

The mayors

The pooled scale includes Bill White (-0.46), Annise Parker (-0.53), Sylvester Turner (-0.61), and John Whitmire (0.24). Turner sits with the Democratic district members who formed his governing majority. Whitmire is nearer the center, alongside Republican-endorsed at-large members elected in 2023. His placement is consistent with the moderate, public-safety and fiscal-restraint themes of his campaign; on the I-45 sale he voted with Republican-affiliated members. White and Parker fall toward the negative side of the pooled dimension, though their precise distance from the later mayors depends on the unresolved historical alignment. Mayors vote on relatively few divided council actions and rarely lose, so these positions describe observed coalitions, not complete governing platforms. Lee P. Brown appears on only two qualifying actions and is excluded by the seven-vote rule.

2024 presidential vote by council district

The plot combines published 2024 precinct results with council-district boundaries. Because many precincts cross district lines, we allocate their votes by the share of precinct area in each district; this assumes voters are spread evenly within each precinct. Among the eleven district seats, Trump share correlates 0.73 with the pooled ideal point. The three most Republican districts, E, G, and A, elected Republican-affiliated district members. F and J are notable exceptions: their members, Thomas and Pollard, lie near the negative end despite comparatively competitive district presidential results. This validates the modern end of the pooled ordering, not the historical link. The small sample and area allocation make it supporting evidence rather than a precise district-level estimate.

Partisan affiliation

Houston’s municipal ballots are nonpartisan, so affiliation comes from external evidence of differing strength: a 2023 Harris County Republican Party endorsement, runoff endorsement, party office, or party-primary candidacy is strongest; a council roster is secondary; reporting or biography alone is weaker. David Robinson and Karla Cisneros have no documented affiliation. We found no winning Houston DSA-endorsed council candidate or formal ideological council caucus, so that validation used for other cities is unavailable here.

Affiliation group In group Others Mean ideal point: group Mean: others
Republican-affiliated (any source) 10 15 0.96 -0.50
Republican party record 7 18 1.08 -0.30
Democratic-affiliated 13 12 -0.49 0.71

Among the 25 members with modern affiliation coding, Republican-affiliated members average 0.96, versus -0.50 for everyone else. A Republican-affiliated member has the higher pooled score in 99% of Republican–non-Republican pairs. The pattern holds when affiliation is restricted to party-record evidence. Dave Martin, classified Republican only from reporting, is a conspicuous exception: he voted with the Turner-era majority. Michael Kubosh, who rejects party labels, falls near the Republican group. These are descriptive checks for the modern subset, not validation of every historical score.

How to read the historical scale

The tabs report the pooled 2003–2026 estimates. They are useful for exploring where people fall on a single candidate scale, but the relationship between older and newer voting blocs is not yet secure. Raising the minimum from two to seven votes per person did not settle that issue. Within-period ordering, especially for the modern council, has stronger support than precise distances between early and recent officials. The plotted intervals condition on the displayed solution and do not cover uncertainty about alternative cross-era alignments. See the technical appendix.

There are genuine overlaps—10 members across 2003–11 and 2012–13, 11 across 2012–13 and 2014–20, and 16 across 2014–20 and 2021–26—but a shared roster does not by itself guarantee a well-determined common ordering. The next substantive checks concern identities and vote coding at the seams and how often the shared members cast informative votes on both sides.

What this pilot shows

The 2003–2026 fit provides a concrete candidate history, including White, Parker, Turner, and Whitmire on one estimated axis. The modern part is well supported by its close agreement with a separate 2021–2026 fit, external party evidence, and district presidential voting. The historical extension is promising but not yet a validated common scale; cross-era distances must be read provisionally. The middle of the council has overlapping uncertainty intervals, and contested votes remain a small, selected part of council business.

Status and limits

This is an exploratory analysis of Jacob’s review-ready, not research-reviewed data candidate. His Houston assessment still marks original-page spot checks, independently established service dates, and two-build reproduction as unresolved. Our three local vote corrections need reconciliation with the upstream parser. The historical identity and scaling checks remain open. This page changes neither the underlying data release nor the earlier Houston report.
